The results of the June 23 primaries seem to confirm that democratic socialists have become, in Harold Meyerson’s apt phrase, the “urban wing” of the Democratic Party. Mamdani’s immense popularity has solidified his position as a kingmaker like no one since the heyday of Carmine DeSapio’s Tammany Hall. Mamdani is not corrupt like Tammany Hall was, of course, but he keeps a sharpened political dagger at hand. He reportedly promised the incumbent congressmember in the thirteenth district, Adriano Espaillat, that he would endorse him for reelection. Espaillat was blindsided when Mamdani instead backed his challenger, Avila Chevalier, a month before the June primary.

Mamdani’s support was important: Avila Chevalier won the nomination by 3.5 percent. But Espaillat’s turf war with established black politicians in Harlem may have been what cost him the election. Prior to Espaillat, Harlem had been the fiefdom of Charles Rangel, a black congressman for forty-six years with national influence and close ties to the Clintons. Some of his protégés continue to hold sway. Avila Chevalier—who, like Espaillat, is Dominican—lost Hispanic voters by 8 percent. But she won black voters by 3.8 percent, almost exactly her margin of victory overall. (White voters favored her by seventeen points.)1 In the end, her victory over a seventy-one-year-old five-term incumbent who pays a great deal of attention to his business enterprises in the district wasn’t entirely surprising.

More divisive in New York was Mamdani’s recruitment of Claire Valdez for the open seat in the seventh congressional district, which runs from Downtown Brooklyn to Woodhaven in Queens. Here, too, his political dagger glinted. For thirty-three years the seat has been held by the hard-fighting progressive Nydia Velázquez, who was close with Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and had been the first member of Congress to endorse Mamdani for mayor. Shortly after Mamdani won last November, Velázquez, seventy-three, announced her retirement, saying that his election bolstered her confidence in the city’s new young political leaders. “I feel at ease,” she told the Times.

Antonio Reynoso, the Brooklyn borough president, was her hand-picked successor. Ignoring the usual courtesies of succession, Mamdani shut Reynoso out in favor of Valdez, a union organizer of steely commitment who had moved to New York from Texas in 2015 to pursue a career in the arts. Reynoso grew up in Los Sures, a Puerto Rican and Dominican neighborhood in Williamsburg within the congressional district. Their political positions were virtually identical: abolish ICE, raise taxes on the rich, oppose US support for Israel’s war crimes in Gaza, and Medicare for All. But their styles are different. Valdez dresses informally, like a union rep on the job, and projects a sense of fire and devotion. Her smile is charismatic and broad. Reynoso is polite, with a mild delivery. He wears the subdued off-the-rack suits of the politician’s trade.

Reynoso had the endorsements of two of New York’s most visible black elected officials, Attorney General Letitia James and Public Advocate Jumaane Williams, as well as that of Velázquez and others. Valdez had the backing and ground game of the DSA. The candidates are essentially of the same generation—Valdez is thirty-six, Reynoso forty-three—but during the campaign Valdez’s camp attacked Reynoso for having taken donations from real estate developers, and the image of Reynoso as a compromised, business-as-usual relic of Brooklyn’s old black political guard stuck. Valdez beat him by twenty points. Apparently Mamdani wants his fellow socialists in power, not just progressives.

Velázquez and James angrily warned the mayor that he could tear apart the progressive coalition that elected him. This remains to be seen. Black political clubs, advocacy groups, and churches have been entrenched in neighborhoods of color in New York City since at least the 1970s. A good example is the Vanguard Independent Democratic Association (VIDA), founded in 1972 and led by the late Al Vann, a black power activist from Bed-Stuy. For decades VIDA wielded a great deal of influence over Central Brooklyn’s political and social life, thanks to its core support from black homeowners. It was entities like VIDA that, five years ago, were critical in helping Eric Adams win the final round of the 2021 mayoral primary by a single point. By ignoring Manhattan below Harlem and predominately white precincts in the boroughs, Adams appeared to carve out a new path to city hall. But in 2026 his coalition seems irrelevant and, in some cases, sclerotic, thanks in part to his administration’s staggering corruption, his self-abasement before Trump to keep himself out of jail, and his administration’s failure to deliver policies of value to New Yorkers.

Advertisement

Mark Winston Griffith, a community organizer in Brooklyn and the former head of the Brooklyn Movement Center in Bed-Stuy, has written incisively about the cultural and psychological tension between neighborhood newcomers and third- or fourth-generation denizens—many of them homeowners—that came to a head on June 23.2 The increasing whitefication of black and Latino strongholds over the past twenty-five years has had an immeasurable effect. Bed-Stuy’s black population dropped from 75 percent in 2000 to 38 percent in 2024. Its white population jumped from 2.4 percent to 33.4 percent in the same period, and that number is rising. Many of VIDA’s black homeowner constituents have sold their appreciated properties and left New York, but the percentage of homeowners in Bed-Stuy has stayed the same at around 20 percent; 78 percent are renters, many of them now white.

As Griffith points out, today we have “Black or brown candidates, most with little to no electoral experience, running against Black or brown Democratic establishment candidates in rapidly changing districts.” All but one of the DSA-endorsed incumbents or insurgent candidates in this cycle were younger than forty. Most of their voters, Griffith suggests, neither know nor care much about their neighborhoods’ black history. What they do know is that they are financially squeezed by suspiciously high gentrified rents and resentful of the status quo. A day or two after the June 23 primary, the writer Molly Crabapple nailed the irony in a tweet:

The politicians whining that DSA voters are “transplants” are the same ones that took real estate cash to greenlight the gentrification of their own communities. These politicians helped displace their own base, then have the gall to complain when new people vote them out.

Political consciousness in New York and elsewhere is spinning away from establishment Democrats. So far, they have offered no answers other than angry denouncements of their rivals (like Carville’s) or lame assurances that they are working against the Trump administration at every turn. They can easily outspend their left-wing challengers: apart from New York City’s staggeringly expensive congressional races, anti-DSA super PACs spent $2.9 million on this year’s state legislative primaries, dwarfing the less than half a million dollars proffered in support of socialist candidates. As Mamdani’s landslide victory over Andrew Cuomo in last year’s mayoral race suggests, however, money doesn’t win elections. Often it hurts candidates who spend it on a mercenary deluge of attacks and robo-ads that turn voters off. At the state level in New York, the DSA will likely pick up at least six new seats in November, giving them fifteen lawmakers between the Assembly and Senate in 2027. That remains a small figure in relative terms: the Senate has sixty-three seats, the Assembly 150. But the organization’s electoral success in NYC is rapidly growing.

The appeal of democratic socialism in other parts of the country is harder to gauge. Highly competitive DSA-endorsed candidates will be running in November for House seats in Denver and Philadelphia, mayor in Los Angeles and Washington, D.C., and a seat in the Kentucky state House in Louisville. The socialist Francesca Hong is polling unexpectedly well in the Democratic primary for governor of Wisconsin, which will take place on August 11. A Republican super PAC is spending $2.2 million on ads to boost Hong’s chances, on the theory that she is too far left to win the general election. Democratic officials in Wisconsin nervously oppose her.

In the Democratic primary for Michigan’s open Senate seat on August 4, Abdul El-Sayed has been polling consistently ahead of his moderate opponent, Haley Stevens. El-Sayed is not a member of the DSA, but his politics align with theirs, especially regarding Israel, which he has called “a rogue state.” AOC has endorsed him, and Politico has reported that DSA officials have “already shifted organizers, volunteers and resources” to Michigan to help him get elected. If either of these candidates wins their primaries, we’ll witness a major test of whether socialists can carry Rust Belt swing states.

These midterms remain volatile. Democrats are flailing for a coherent message that will resonate with voters, while Republicans seem set to pay for their spectacular dystopian failures. Aware of the danger and with an eye on his own presidential prospects in 2028, J.D. Vance told the podcaster Joe Rogan recently that, “crazy” as socialism is, it’s a natural response to the “extreme wealth inequality” in the US economy. Unless young Americans “own something [like their homes], socialism is the inevitable outcome.” Vance, the promotional product of tech billionaires with Übermensch delusions, meant this as a cautionary statement, not a proposal that Republicans back a universal platform.

Jaime Harrison, the former chair of the Democratic National Committee, recently sent a warning to socialists:

If you hate the Democratic Party, then please don’t run for our nomination. Don’t use our resources. Don’t rely on our volunteers. Don’t use our infrastructure. Focus on building the party you actually support.

Never mind that the DSA supplies its own volunteers—if Harrison were to be heeded, Democrats would run the risk of shrinking into permanent irrelevance. They would do better to welcome socialists into the party and to adopt some of their ideas, which are no more radical than Social Security was during the New Deal. Our two major parties have moved so far to the right since 1980 that common-sense proposals to rebalance the economy are met with terror, as if they will turn the US into a twenty-first-century version of the Soviet Union. But Democrats currently have no path to becoming the majority party without making room for an outspoken and unambiguous left flank.

Two years ago, during the 2024 Democratic primary for the assembly seat in my Crown Heights district, a neighbor wanted to know more about the incumbent, Stefani Zinerman, before casting her ballot. Did she count real estate developers among her donors? Zinerman’s office wouldn’t answer the question. My neighbor cast her ballot for Eon Huntley, the DSA-sponsored candidate, who was an active parent in the local public schools.

Like all DSA candidates, Huntley accepts no money from large corporations, real estate developers, or special interests. That year he lost by 516 votes. In June, when he ran against Zinerman again, he won by more than twenty points. Voters like my neighbor long for representatives who haven’t been bought, and the DSA has provoked them to scrutinize those who have been. The rubber stamp that political machines have counted on has been withdrawn.

—July 23, 2026

entries.title: Refusing to Look Away
entries.summary: In Killing Spree, the poet Jorie Graham pursues an essentially ethical impulse to find a true language for the evil in the world.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Setting out, in September 1800, to define the character of the poet for a new age, William Wordsworth came to the conclusion that good poems could be written only by someone “who, being possessed of more than usual organic sensibility, had also thought long and deeply.” Most of us live at the mercy of our routines. We punch the clock, fret over deadlines, and fall into the algorithmic trap of doomscrolling, swiping past headline after headline, reel after reel, each bearing the day’s report of calamity and outrage. We self-soothe with empty calories: The Real Housewives, romantasy, and chill. Wordsworth’s era was different in degree but not in kind. Overwhelmed by news of foreign wars and economic collapse, his contemporaries had been reduced “to a state of almost savage torpor,” living on a toxic diet of “frantic novels, sickly and stupid German Tragedies, and deluges of idle and extravagant stories in verse.”

The poet would have to resist “this degrading thirst after outrageous stimulation.” He would remind his readers “what is really important to men,” cultivating their capacity for serious, sustained inquiry and moral reflection. At the same time, he would have to remain alert to the catastrophes of the present, which for Wordsworth was defined by the rapid corrosion of traditional ways of life brought on by industrial capitalism. Because the poet feels and sees so much more than others do, because he understands both the historical present and the human condition with greater sympathy and precision than the average person, it is his job to act as our collective psychologist, healer, and sage. (So convinced was Wordsworth of his own powers in this regard that he sent copies of his book to several “persons of eminence,” including the prominent politician Charles Fox, hoping to convince them to do something about poverty and social collapse, about the destruction of English forests and the metastatic “spreading of manufactures” across the land. Fox replied that he liked the poems that rhymed, the blank verse not so much.)

It would be hard to find a contemporary American poet who embodies the Wordsworthian ideal as fully as Jorie Graham. Her work, shaped and driven by its own “more than usual organic sensibility,” pursues an essentially ethical impulse to reinvigorate our perception of the world, to wean us from exhausted and exhausting habits of mind and train us in vital new ones. It is allergic in equal measure to stupidity and cruelty, and as compassionate toward its readers as toward the figures, both human and animal, that populate its lines. A good way to summarize Graham’s project might be to say that she, like Wordsworth, is ever alert to the fact that the root of aesthetics is aesthesis, or sensation, and that poetry is concerned first and foremost with, in his words, “the general passions and thoughts and feelings of men” and “the moral sentiments” arising from them.

In 2022 four of Graham’s recent books were published together in the collection [To] The Last [Be] Human, a climate change quartet that gives itself the painful task of bearing witness to present-tense grief at the disappearance of normal weather and to the anticipatory terror of a ruined future. The poems in those books are rich with prosopopoeia, a rhetorical device whereby a nonhuman entity is given the power of speech. “The earth said/remember me,” one of them begins. “The earth said/don’t let go.” Graham obeys her own elegiac imperative, put in the mouth of an abstract yet eerily intimate presence, and gives herself over to the lyric memorialization of birds, trees, grass, potable water, “cod larvae” that will not hatch, their lives aborted by rising ocean temperatures. She fulfills the mandate of her title: If we are to be the last humans, we must also be human to the last, using our species’ unique capacity for meaning-making to mourn what we might have avoided losing but have lost all the same.

In Killing Spree, her latest collection, Graham’s notes change to tragic. Her laments are now laced with fury, as genocidal wars and murderous technologies join global warming in the twenty-first century’s third decade. Most appalling to Graham is our collective inertia, not to say apathy. The world “didn’t change much/at first,” she writes in the book’s first poem, and neither did we. “Where is everyone,” she asks, before being met by a terrifying stillness, at once the silence of mass death (“Only just heard/no one survived”) and the stupefaction or indifference of those who feel, for now, untouched by mounting crises. For all its characteristic restraint and formal diligence, Killing Spree is a book that wants to make noise, to cut through the dead air with cries of grief and rage, undoing our own savage torpor. Graham knows that it might make no difference; poetry, as we are often reminded, makes nothing happen. But she also knows that a difference—even just a minor variation in what we notice and how—is the only thing a poem can make.

Born in 1950 as Jorie Pepper, Graham is the daughter of the journalist Curtis Bill Pepper and the acclaimed sculptor Beverly Stoll Pepper, whose large-scale creations in iron and stone can be found all over the world, from the town of Assisi in central Italy to Barcelona, Calgary, and New Jersey. Graham studied philosophy at the Sorbonne and filmmaking at NYU before earning her MFA at the Iowa Writers’ Workshop, to which she returned to teach; in 1999 she became Harvard’s Boylston Professor of Rhetoric and Oratory. (She was the first woman to occupy the position, which she held until 2025.) Graham is, to say the least, decorated, the recipient of innumerable awards and honors. Thirty years ago a volume of her poems called The Dream of the Unified Field won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry, for which her fifteenth book, To 2040 (2023), was also a finalist.

According to the late critic Helen Vendler, Graham began “as a writer of short poems in short lines, lines with a hesitant rhythm so seductive that one’s heart, reproducing those poems, almost found a new way to beat.” Her style then changed or, to use Vendler’s word, broke. “With a burst of almost tidal energy,” Vendler wrote, Graham started composing “long poems in long lines, poems that pressed toward an excess nearly uncontainable by the page.” In the American poetic tradition, the long line is most closely associated with Whitman, who used it as a wildly self-expressive and hortatory form. But while she likes the long line, Graham is equally interested in the figurative possibilities of orthography. Her lines are sliced and diced by ellipses, brackets, abbreviations (“yr,” “&”), blanks, elongated underscores, rightward arrows, and most notably em dashes, whose prosodic as well as rhetorical possibilities remain essential to her form.

The em dash is Graham’s most recognizable poetic device. To speak technically for a moment, the em dash introduces a caesura—a cut or a break—into the line, which naturally suggests a slackening of its momentum, though how long that pause ought to last is an open question. Unlike a period, a comma, or a semicolon, the em dash is mercurial in its meaning. It can suggest rupture or connection, and although its visual presence on the page is conspicuous, it also implies something hidden, a thought that will not or cannot be expressed in words and instead makes itself known only through the vocal hitch of a lightly held breath. It is a penumbra, a partial occlusion of sense.

The key word here is partial. The founding conceit of the modern lyric poem is that it gives us unfettered access to the innermost thoughts and feelings of the poem’s speaker, who is often taken (rightly or wrongly) to be the poem’s author. Lyric, in the words of Jonathan Culler, is the “dramatized experience of a consciousness,” neither an argument nor a confession but the record of a mind “attempting to come to terms with the fundamental aspects of the human condition, as embodied in the situation confronting it.” Graham accepts the premise but thwarts its more banal implications. When her dashes appear, it is often to provide a graphic representation of the remoteness and opacity of another person’s mind, to convey privacy where the lyric would encourage or presume disclosure. Here is Graham in her 2017 collection Fast, describing a medical procedure:

my body, my citizen, anesthesiologists back from coffee break, cables



on mylar headrest taking my head down now, arms into armlock,

then positioners, restraints—day talk

all round—the guidewires in, the intravenous ports, the drip begun.

An/aesthesia by which is meant the sensation of having sensation blocked.

a collapse of response, a total lack of awareness of loss of awareness—

on the wall, snapshots of the chosen few training on



the new

robotic patient-

lookalikes

The poem’s title, “Prying,” recasts surgery as a revelation under duress: the doctors do not open up the body so much as snoop and root around in it. Rather than “memories, contritions, facts,” and all the other immaterial things that make a person a person, their quarry is the “rapid over-rhyming cells” of disease. In the face of this incursion—brutal but necessary—the patient retreats into herself as “day talk” buzzes “all round” her, the dashes on either side of that phrase (before “day” and after “round”) affording her a slender, tinny privacy, like the curtain around a hospital bed. A few lines later, the dash signifies the lapse of “awareness” that follows its anesthetic “loss”; in the poem’s last line, “And you get a little extra life to live now—here—can you still live it,” the speaker comes to in the enclosure of “here,” this place where a little more life is available, if she can stand it.

Advertisement

All this is to say that Graham is a poet who consistently confounds her own self-representation, withdrawing from testimony even when she lays herself bare. Not for her the torrential unbosoming of so much contemporary lyric, with its mawkish self-regard and biographical appetites. Dramatizing the experience of one’s consciousness is only worthwhile (or, to use Wordsworth’s phrase, “really important”) if that consciousness is capable of understanding itself as operating within a shared historical condition, independent and idiosyncratic but nonetheless irreducibly in dialogue with other minds or essences. The broken line, the hard scar of the dash—these are gestures toward the uncertain and intractable distance between self and other, presence and absence, “awareness” and its loss.

Graham’s language hovers at a breaking point. It is erudite and self-assured, but it has an underlying fragility that suggests someone trying to hold back a tide of chaos and disintegration. Like Paul Celan, Graham wants to know what it sounds like when meaning gives way to the malignant jabber of history, or when it is so overcome by its own futility that it sinks into silence. Sentences are more often fragmented than not—“Midwinter. Dead of,” begins the poem “Futures”—and almost always elliptical, as if unwilling to impose intelligibility on a world that makes so little sense. Words are left to drift across the poem’s surface like a swan that appears “out of nowhere on [a] drying river,” sick but still floating. The effect produces a kind of frustrated empathy: the reader identifies with Graham’s speaker but also feels impossibly far from her, locked as she is in her own grief for all the dying birds and desiccated waters. The poet’s voice, to borrow a phrase from Celan, is “no one’s voice, again.” Faint but familiar, it is trying to stay with us, in snatches and shards, to speak for as long as it can, to whoever cares to listen.

The voice of Killing Spree is intimate and communal—not a specific person but an exemplary one. “This//first person/I use here,” Graham writes, is “a way of referring/to my being in//abeyance.” Her pronouns tack between “I,” “we,” and “you” or sometimes “u,” and her poems are mostly shorn of what would look like biography: no more dispatches from the hospital ward. Rather, we find ourselves in a nightmarish world peopled by figures with allegorical heft—mothers, fathers, priests, a prime minister “watching a disaster movie.” Like Alice Notley’s The Descent of Alette (1992) and, more recently, Annelyse Gelman’s Vexations (2023), Killing Spree represents the experience of living in a dystopia as both intensely isolating and strangely, relentlessly public. The lyric “I” is turned inside out, as private preoccupations are usurped by the collective experience of watching the world burn. “Now and again,” Graham writes in that first poem, “The World,”

your soul



wakes up in

spurts asking

what is—or is there—a just

struggle. Then you,

then I, cry out

where are you

everyone. We were in one world

& then was it u or

us or them or no one in

particular—in

particular, my heart

leaps at that—oh

in particular

Vendler found Graham’s mode of inhabiting the lyric “magisterially impersonal,” and therefore well equipped to represent “what used to be called the soul”: the part of ourselves that is not reducible to “personal circumstance” but roves freely beyond and even transcends it. In “The World,” the soul is abbreviated by flatulent “spurts” and the text-message shorthand of “u.” It is no longer “particular” but digitized and diffuse, the whole idea of particularity—of an unreplicable uniqueness—becoming something like a memory. There is an obvious allusion to Wordsworth’s poem “My Heart Leaps Up,” written in 1802, the day before the poet composed his more famous “Ode: Intimations of Immortality from Recollections of Early Childhood.” As Graham knows, “My Heart Leaps Up” is the easy, innocent overture to the melancholy and complex ode, to which the earlier poem lends its last three lines as an epigraph. In the first poem, the poet rejoices at his own love for nature, at his ability to take unmediated pleasure in the beauty of a rainbow. “So was it when my life began,” he assures us. “So is it now I am a man.”

The ode abandons the trusting singsong of “My Heart Leaps Up” and its blithe faith in what Wordsworth calls “natural piety.” The speaker of this poem recognizes the beauty of “meadow, grove, and stream,” but being an adult beset by all sorts of neuroses, he no longer perceives them with unmixed delight. “It is not now as it hath been of yore,” Wordsworth writes. “The things which I have seen I now can see no more.” Killing Spree likewise situates itself at a time when “there hath past away a glory from the earth,” not because Graham, at the age of seventy-six, is no longer an artless appreciator of the natural world but because nature itself is “no more.” Wordsworth’s “Fountains, Meadows, Hills, and Groves” are being replaced by data centers. “The mountain,” Graham writes in “Then the Fog,” “is cleaved open./The silver is picked out.” “Are those humans out there,” she wonders, “or/just hollows filled with mercury & ash.”

If Killing Spree were merely a lament for a greener, cooler, unpoisoned planet it would still be full of beautiful poems, but it would not achieve the moral sublimity that Graham does. This is a book in which ecocide and genocide go hand in hand, as they do in real life. Several of Graham’s poems appear to be set in Gaza, where war has severely polluted the water and soil. (I say they appear to be set in Gaza although, of course, the location might also be Lebanon or Iran.) “The Zero Point” describes a father in a tent with his son just after the tent is hit by a missile. Graham addresses this father as “you” and also speaks of him in the third person, as if to remind the reader that it is only thanks to an accident of history that she is sitting somewhere in safety, reading a book of poetry, while thousands of miles away some of the world’s wealthiest nations cheerfully drop bombs on refugee camps:

the zero point



where you call

into the face of

your child

which does not move,

the zero

of its lid you’re pushing up

seeking the gaze—

just look

at me, look

back at me its father is

screaming, the zero

where he only finds

a hand, a part

of the arm, where he picks them up—

…Here’s his foot now



in this dust.

The fire picks it out.

It looks like

it’s running.

Graham may have become known as a poet of long lines, but here her phrases are preemptively slivered, each thought or address (“just look/at me”) cut off before it finds safe passage to its end. Along with that telling movement between grammatical persons, there is the choice to sometimes refer to the child as “it” (as in, “its father”) and other times to make clear that the child is male: the last lines of the poem are “Hold your tongue, fire.//Hold your fire.//Let my boy run.” The shift allows the child to serve, perhaps, as a symbol of all such children—shot, bombed, burned alive—while remaining singular, a child who, like any child, was someone’s entire universe.

“The Zero Point” chimes agonizingly with the Palestinian poet Mosab Abu Toha’s “For a Moment,” published in his collection Forest of Noise (2024). Abu Toha’s speaker carries a young girl in his arms; he knows she is dead (“The pressure of the explosion/tore apart her thin veins”), but “everyone who sees us,” he says, “runs after us.” “You are alive/for a moment,” Abu Toha concludes, “when living people/run after you.” Both poems are part of an emerging body of literature written during the Gaza genocide, and they share certain formal features—that slippage between the first, second, and third person—as well as a thematic emphasis on the fate of children during wartime. Graham similarly counters the paralysis of death with an image of limbs in motion. The little boy’s foot, sheared off his body, looks like it’s running; the crowd runs after the man cradling the dead girl, who, suspended in a collective fantasy of her survival, cannot yet be grieved.

To say that a life is grievable, according to the philosopher Judith Butler, is to recognize that its loss matters. Such recognition is not sentimental but social and political: it decides who counts as part of the human community. But Butler goes further: “Without grievability, there is no life, or, rather, there is something living that is other than life.” If our lives do not matter we are not really living; we are enduring, and to uncertain purpose. Graham’s poems grieve not from within the passivity of despair but with the intention of upholding the value both of lives lost and of lives that have not been lived so much as survived. Killing Spree puts into words what many of Graham’s fellow Americans have yet to understand, namely that the condition of being ungrievable—precarious, disposable—in the eyes of those who wield the drones and the jets and the hypersonic missiles might at any moment be shared by those who now feel well cushioned by privilege and security. “No One Today,” a poem whose first line is also its title, begins “of my own died.”

Beloveds



were not dragged

into the net of

the eye of

the drone, were not dis-

membered into

instant ancestors—

not even memories—too

fast, too torn, no. Screams.

Yet despite the speaker’s apparent safety, there is the intimation of being “suddenly” down in

the burning



mounds the slippery

pits—how did our room

disappear—& is that a

cry under there, is that a hand

opening and

shutting—a piece of

skin

“Where//are my things,” the speaker asks, “the/things I loved.” With this utterance she seems tolled back (as Keats says) to her sole self, touching the green of spring grass and reminding herself that “no arm is being/amputated” from the people she cares for, “no rib-//cage crushed,” “no body loved beyond/measure growing//limp here.” But the consolation is a mirage. In the next several lines, the speaker begs some silent other to wake up and let her feed it, give it milk, sing it a song—but this other is dead, the mute addressee of an unwitting apostrophe, its eyelids stuck open, its limbs unnaturally bent.

Amputation is a good word for what this book fears most—not just a physical dismemberment but also the severing of persons from their own humanity. In the twenty-first century the indiscriminate massacre of civilians is joined, almost necessarily, by the evisceration of our lives by technology. It’s not a coincidence that the CEO of the music-streaming service Spotify recently invested $700 million in Helsing, a company that develops AI software for military use. All day, every day, we find ourselves vaporized into data, inscribed into a parodic collectivity in which

We are all breathing here together, are we not?



We are all leaking our in-

formation, our attentiveness….

Connect with me. How many things can we pay attention to at



once. How many. Track me. Track my

proclivities. Harvest me. My gaze is my gift. I give it, I give it to you

freely.

Compare this “gift” with the gaze that is sought and not found in “The Zero Point,” as the father pushes up his dead child’s lids, looking in vain for a sign of life. This is the gaze of one who says, in Graham’s words, “I will be yr/user,” a phrase that is at once erotically charged and bloodless, as are the sinister promises that precede it: “Here is my open eye for you, I will en-/counter you, I will rub the personal surface, I will skim it.” From the eternally open eye of surveillance software to the shuttered eyes of the boy blown to bits in his tent is not a small step; it is not even a step. There is only one kind of machine, and it is built for war.

What is to be done? With its last poem, Killing Spree achieves something like grace—mangled and thin but unfaltering. “Am I//thinking straight/on this page,” Graham wonders, a page “which I can’t hold/anymore, which u/still can?” She asks the reader to “raise yr voice in my voice” or else to “raise my voice in yrs,” for “what remains is//always, only, voice.” This is as strong a claim for poetry as any I have heard, deeply affecting in both its clarity and its desperation. In her final lines, Graham borrows a refrain from Ezra Pound’s Pisan Cantos to reassure us, and herself, that “what thou lovest well/remains,” thus proving Pound’s point that “What thou lov’st well is thy true heritage… What thou lov’st well shall not be reft from thee.” This century, having taken so much from so many, will go on with its program of graft, plunder, butchery, and terrorism. We should not ask ourselves what we can do to survive it. Instead we should ask, as Graham does, “What have I done” and, more importantly, “Who will I become.” To carry poetry inside us always, to raise its voice, is the beginning of an answer.

Waiting for a call that didn’t happen



I am sitting on the back porch with Frank O’Hara (Collected)

when a goldfinch lands beside my head on the porch rail,

lands so neatly so instantly so whoosh

with all his yellowness yellowing

and all his himness packed to the brim of him

that a wave of coolness

comes past my left cheek as surprise cool as

a word we don’t have a word for

or my left cheek briefly

blue.

entries.content:
The nightjar carries it lightly



But the world’s heavy as a lamp in a gale.

I watched it move through the olives and the hush,

Over rooftops, stones, and cragged hills,

Unclenched as it glistens in the gloam,

Indifferent, sonorous, and true.

As I write, a fly has drowned



In my jar of pungent lit wax,

Its carcass still dancing from its thrash

In the melt pool.

A galaxy of smoke spirals from the wick,



Rearranging itself, then unspooling

Out and over the valley’s scruff of lavender and tobacco

To resume its argument with the bird



About death. And once more

The bird wins by saying nothing,

Which is inevitable and enough.

entries.content:
Some friends call mine a spiritual problem



and when they do

I become the minister of the real

and go on Zillow

moving my future into various crannies of Los Angeles.

When one friend calls returning home

more practical,

I find myself in our yard

under a colander of stars, tasting

pasta I might never make again

the way he likes it, naked

with flake-salt and oil. I am the moon

for him only rarely. But when I am

I am the one who changes.

entries.title: A Gust from Another World
entries.summary: The Search for Bridey Murphy caused a sensation in 1950s America, and while its tale of reincarnation was soon discredited, it revealed a deep cultural fascination with the supernatural.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
This article appeared in slightly different form in Critique (June–July 2025) as “L’hypnotiseur et la revenante: sur une autre tendance du noir.”

It was at the lowest of decibels that the voice of Bridey Murphy—muffled, groggily articulated—leaked into America. Bridey first made herself heard on the night of November 29, 1952, in a living room in Pueblo, Colorado, elicited from Virginia “Ginni” Tighe through the ministrations of Morey Bernstein, an amateur hypnotist. Ginni was the twenty-nine-year-old wife of a local Oldsmobile dealer; Morey, when not engaged with his hobby, ran a profitable family business specializing in heavy equipment for farms and ranches.

He had been enthralled with hypnosis for a decade. At first applying it to the treatment of headaches, insomnia, and stuttering, he was drawn gradually into uncharted realms: precognition, telepathy, clairvoyance, and finally reincarnation, something he had once regarded as “preposterous” but was now eager to investigate and, if possible, document. He had tried his hand at hypnotic age regression and was confident that he had taken subjects back to early childhood. Now he wondered whether the process could be pushed further, perhaps into a previous existence. Ginni, a casual acquaintance, seemed an ideal candidate for the experiment. In a few earlier sessions he had been struck by “how quickly and deeply she had become entranced…. Furthermore, she had remembered absolutely nothing afterward…. She was, in short, a somnambulistic subject.”* Ginni had agreed to hypnosis as a treatment for allergies and had no interest in revisiting past lives.

With his tape recorder running, Morey led her “back through time and space, just like turning back in the pages of a book,” all the way to age one, before venturing “over the hump,” as he later described it (using the World War II term for the trans-Himalayan route from India to China), instructing her that “there are other scenes from faraway lands and distant places in your memory…and when I talk to you again you will tell me about it.” Within moments she identified herself as what sounded at first like “Friday Murphy,” a small child living in Cork in Ireland in “eighteen something…1806.” Her hair was red; her father was a barrister; her younger brother had died of “some kind of black something”; she had muffins and jam for breakfast; her husband’s favorite dish was boiled beef with onions. So it went on, for this and five further sessions, as Morey teased out details of Bridey’s fairly uneventful life one fragment at a time: her childhood amusements, her marriage, her relocation from Cork to Belfast, her death in 1864 after a fall down the stairs (“Seems I broke some bones in my hip too”), her funeral (“I watched them ditch my body”), her lingering in the house alongside her husband, who couldn’t see or hear her, her subsequent stay in a place where time “doesn’t mean anything…no night or no day.”

Shared at first among acquaintances for whom Morey was eager to play the tapes, news of the sessions spread to a wider audience through a series of articles in The Denver Post. When his own account, The Search for Bridey Murphy, was published with great fanfare in January 1956, it quickly became the best-selling book in America. The paperback edition, rushed into print soon after, splashed across its cover the question “DOES THIS BOOK PROVE LIFE AFTER DEATH?”

The details about Bridey that Morey had elicited were not very exciting—in fact they were unrelievedly drab, pieces of an obscure life without great drama and with only minor pleasures, in a country more monochrome and sullen than the Ireland of movies. This made the book all the more plausible. Its most devoted readers were women, whose interest in prenatal regression, Morey noted, “is definitely keener than that of men.” Some may have found comfort in the idea that a life so enclosed and frustrated was not the end but merely a prelude to something better: something perhaps like Ginni’s as a reasonably affluent housewife in the Sun Belt whose weekly round of bridge games and cocktail parties may have seemed as much a fantasy as her phantasmal former existence.

The phenomenon of Bridey Murphy—a gust of wind from another world—for a moment nudged aside communism, juvenile delinquency, and the ascendancy of Elvis Presley. Hypnotists were suddenly much in demand, and a good many readers lined up to uncover their own past lives. At least one death was blamed on the book, the suicide of a nineteen-year-old Oklahoman who wrote that he was “curious about the Bridey Murphy story” and was going to investigate. There was a flurry of novelty songs: “The Ballad of Bridey Murphy,” “The Bridey Murphy Rock and Roll,” “Do You Believe in Reincarnation.” Liberace incorporated a Bridey routine into his stage show. Bernstein released excerpts from the hypnotic sessions on LP. A movie version starring Teresa Wright and Louis Hayward (“A Sensational Story of Hypnosis from the Year’s Best Seller”) was released by Paramount in October, with other films about reincarnation and hypnotism tagging along (Richard Bartlett’s I’ve Lived Before, Edward L. Cahn’s The She-Creature, Roger Corman’s The Undead).

Advertisement

Traces of Bridey Murphy turn up everywhere in the archives of 1956. There was something for everybody to feed on. The scandal magazine Uncensored asks the question “Phoney or Phenom?,” while Top Secret promises to expose “The Bridey Murphy Hoax.” Detractors and debunkers (scientists, theologians, investigative reporters) emerge on all sides. John R. Cavanaugh assures readers of The Catholic Standard and Times that “the solid reality of the truths of the Catholic Faith” offers a sure defense against “such an ancient superstition as metempsychosis.” The Catholic intellectual William F. Buckley, on the other hand, in his newly founded National Review, hopes that the Bridey revelations might put a dent in America’s “Age of Materialism.” William Bernard Ready, in The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction, decries “the downright dullness and tastelessness that emanate…like an effluvium…. It is a grave reflection upon the state of society.”

Mockery abounds. Time describes Ginni’s voice on the recording as “somewhat like a savagely beaten gun moll who is being quizzed by the opposition gang.” In a parody of TV Guide, Mad magazine has Bridey starring in the movie drama You Only Live Twice. The Bowery Boys comedy Hold That Hypnotist exposes the best-selling author of The Previous Life of Sally Klingle (“We’ve all lived before. Who were you?”) as a scam artist in league with gangsters. Disney’s Uncle Scrooge McDuck is “levitated” to a past life by a financially strapped hypnotist whose bookshelves include Quest for Tidie Brophy, Search for Lydie Burfee, and Paging Gracie Macy. The pop satirist of the hour, Stan Freberg, releases the hit comedy record “The Quest for Bridey Hammerschlaugen,” with Freberg’s hypnotist sounding suspiciously like Senator Joe McCarthy (“Remember you’re under oath here”). But the book sold and sold.

A year later the fever had subsided. The movie—a glum and threadbare production—had flopped. Research in Ireland had turned up little to confirm and much to cast doubt on the Bridey narrative, and when the Chicago American tracked down a childhood neighbor of Ginni’s named Bridie Murphy Corkell, it looked like a definitive indication that the story’s specifics came from nowhere but Ginni’s own past and imagination. Her past turned out to be more troubled and complicated than the book had revealed—she had been raised by relatives after her parents (both in fact part Irish) split up when she was three, and a brief first marriage had ended with her husband’s death in World War II. Estranged relatives, some offended by the religious implications of the story, went public with discrediting information. As for her imagination and the reading that fed it, it was evidently more extensive than Morey had let on or even suspected. At the time he had written in a private letter, “She just can’t be making these things up…. How could a hypnotized gal—just an everyday young married gal, with no special education or theatrical turn of mind—dream up this stuff?”

Cryptomnesia was the deflating term deployed to explain where those details had come from. Hypnotic subjects were obedient; they wanted to please the hypnotist. Ginni was simply dreaming out loud, with an external dream master providing the cues and steering her improvisations along more or less regulated pathways. The Bridey Murphy story drifted away, ceding the spotlight to another narrative uncovered by hypnosis, again a best seller turned rapidly into a movie, The Three Faces of Eve (1957), with its unsettling and sexually charged revelations of multiple personalities (“Three Women in One Body!”).

I was seven when Bernstein’s book was published and can recall the stir it made among my contemporaries, as it filtered down from the adult world through kitchen conversations and magazine covers. The tale spread by word of mouth, just as it must have been retold and embellished all over the country. We couldn’t easily shake off its suggestion of a spooky underworld in which people migrated from one life to another through a gray intermediary zone inhabited by a transient population of the temporarily dead. It seemed as if the story had to be true—Ginni remembered things she could not possibly have known about—since the details were alleged in the retelling to match up uncannily with verified facts.

For my father, when I asked him about it, the answer was simple: “They’re all fakes.” All of them: mediums, mentalists, fortune-tellers, faith healers, charismatic preachers, door-to-door encyclopedia salesmen. He had come of age in the 1930s and had no use for the otherworldly. A hard-edged skepticism had been in the American air for a long time, pushing against the recurring prevalence of one credulous enthusiasm after another. The debunking spirit could be found in Mark Twain, in H.L. Mencken, in pulp detective stories in which all seers and swamis were invariably fraudulent, and in a good many early 1930s movies—Warren William as the carnival psychic Chandra the Great (a name borrowed from the label on a cookie wrapper) in The Mind Reader (1933), Barbara Stanwyck as the fake evangelist in The Miracle Woman (1931), Boris Karloff as the tabloid reporter disguised as a minister in Five Star Final (1931). Himself an entertainer (his morning radio show had become popular), my father saw the realm of mystical rigmarole as at best another branch of show business. At worst it was systematic fraud or something even more sinister, the kind of delusional doctrine that could send nations down evil paths.

Advertisement

In truth no adult males I knew showed much interest in the eerie or irrational. We lived in a community grounded in practicalities, reassured by material things that functioned: fuse boxes, automobile engines, lawn mowers, power drills, reel-to-reel tape recorders. Popular Mechanics was sold in every drugstore. In a world brightly lit and logically organized there was nowhere for ghosts to hide. Death itself seemed to exist elsewhere, in a kind of exile. For the voice of Bridey Murphy to slip into that world suggested a blast from the country of the dead through a gap not even suspected.

What seemed to authenticate it, at least in children’s eyes, was a long article in Life: “Bridey Murphy Puts Nation in a Hypnotizzy.” The title was whimsical, and the small print laid out the debunking counterarguments, but for us Life was all about the pictures. Each week, in photos and meticulously detailed paintings, we were given beauty contests and battlefields, rock-and-roll parties and H-bomb tests, dinosaurs and Kim Novak, Winston Churchill and lunar craters. No columns of half-understood prose (“Here Are Facts…Here Are Opinions of Scientists”) could undermine the photograph of Morey Bernstein leaning over Ginni Tighe with a lighted candle. Morey’s shadow was cast on the wall like a night-wandering doppelgänger, and the candle radiated hypnotic power from the very paper on which the magazine was printed. If this was happening in a living room, it was not like any living rooms we knew.

So many dark and ancient currents converged in such an image. Reincarnation was ungraspable. How could we conceive of it when death itself was unreal? Of hypnotism we knew only a few trappings, which we incorporated into playground games. The archetype of the hypnotist with his sonorous incantations (“Look into my eyes…. You are getting sleepy”) melded in imagination with the magician in top hat and cape. (Mandrake the Magician was still to be found on the funny pages in those days.) There was no ignoring the ads in the back of comic books: “Want the thrill of imposing your will over someone? Of making someone do exactly what you order? Try hypnotism!” “Amaze friends—Exert your Hypnotic Power over others—Be POPULAR and WANTED!” The suggestiveness of the crude drawing of a pop-eyed young man directing his gaze toward a woman in a low-cut red dress, with a convenient couch in the background, may have been a bit lost on us. But the sinister aura of the mesmerist’s commanding eyes was inescapable, even if we only vaguely sensed what ends that command might serve.

One would have to regress like a somnambulist to trace these figures back to their buried sources. The desire to do that became strong; it might be a project for a lifetime, with a marvelous or terrifying secret uncovered at the end. Hints were scattered everywhere. I became aware that my Irish grandmother—who was nine years old when George du Maurier’s Trilby was published in 1894—still shivered at the name of Svengali, the very prototype of the malevolent hypnotist, who had turned the untalented working girl Trilby into a world-famous singer through the power of suggestion before vengefully wrenching the gift away. The worldwide fascination stirred by Trilby had embedded Svengali in the language and kept him alive in plays and movies, while the character’s elements of explicit antisemitic caricature were gradually scrubbed away.

Meanwhile my Hungarian grandmother, who had a taste for uncanny explanations, subscribed to Fate magazine, with its “true stories of the strange and the unknown”; the November 1956 cover story was “Bridey Murphy in Ireland: A Personal Investigation.” Rummaging in the back of a closet I found a Ouija board that had been hers and learned that my mother and her sister when young had experimented in contacting spirits with it. There was no end of histories to be excavated: the lore of spells and séances, hexes and black sabbaths, the magic circles of Faust and Dr. Dee, the magnetic wonders of Cagliostro and Mesmer, the newly revealed wisdom of Madame Blavatsky and the Hidden Masters, exotic cults of Africa and Asia, buried scrolls of drowned civilizations, occultists calling up pagan and demonic powers, obsessed scientists stumbling on undreamed-of metamorphoses.

They melted readily into a grand olio that generated infinite variants, whether in the fantastic novels of H. Rider Haggard and Sax Rohmer and Dennis Wheatley or the extravagant horror and fantasy comic books that by 1956 had been suppressed by censorship. Cinema above all was the natural domain for this infusion of the unreal into the visible. Movies did not merely depict trances, they induced them. The hypnotist continually returned, his entrancing stare in close-up holding the audience itself enraptured. The gazes of hypnotist and subject were riveted together in a frequently replicated two-shot—subject (generally female) leaning backward, hypnotist (almost exclusively male) bending forward in a predatory crouch—that mirrored the relation of spectator to screen. From the Central European homeland of Mesmer and Freud came Dr. Caligari—sinister sideshow entertainer, master of mind control, deranged psychiatrist—traveling through splintered streetscapes with his murderous coffin-dwelling somnambule Cesare.

The “real” Caligari, as clarified in the film’s epilogue, was a benevolent asylum director who had become the subject of his patient’s paranoid delusions. But the confusion hardly mattered; the story could just as easily be turned around, as it would be so often, laying bare the malice and madness of outwardly respectable psychological theorists. Whatever distinctions might exist among science and the supernatural and the merely fraudulent—among psychoanalysis, mesmerism, yoga, demonic mischief, astral projection, fairground trickery, and elaborate criminal conspiracy—were blurred sufficiently to disappear. Fritz Lang’s Dr. Mabuse in 1922 is at once psychoanalyst, hypnotist, occultist, charlatan, crime lord, and finally certified lunatic; by 1933, in The Testament of Dr. Mabuse, he does not even need a body, the power of suggestion having made his clinical custodian the vehicle of his will operating beyond the grave. Irresistible disembodied will permeates space.

When Morey Bernstein was in his teens, movie theaters were full of suggestive hints. Marian Marsh succumbed to the mesmeric power of John Barrymore in Svengali (1931). Madge Bellamy in White Zombie (1932) and Dorothy Burgess in Black Moon (1934) became the mental slaves of voodoo practitioners. Myrna Loy in Thirteen Women (1932) was a Eurasian woman unleashing hypnotic skills to avenge the snubs of her racist sorority sisters. In Supernatural (1933) Carole Lombard was possessed by the spirit of a dead murderess. These were not fantasies entirely divorced from surrounding realities. Speaking in Munich in 1936, Adolf Hitler declared, “I go the way that Providence dictates with the assurance of a sleepwalker.” The mass spectacles of fascism suggested to some Americans an emerging army of blindly obedient somnambules. During the war years a corresponding legion of ritualists, amnesiacs, and zombies stalked the shadow realm of movies. Irrational forces exercised their power through inexorable European curses (Cat People, Cry of the Werewolf), unholy medical experiments (Captive Wild Woman, The Lady and the Monster), and diabolist cults (The Seventh Victim, Weird Woman).

Mind control in one form or another continued to haunt the postwar dreamscape, with scientists as likely to be perpetrators as saviors. A psychologist is possessed by the mind of an executed killer (The Phantom Speaks, 1945); the director of a prestigious sanatorium is a deranged murderer (Spellbound, 1945); a psychiatrist conspires with a carnival mentalist whom she ultimately destroys (Nightmare Alley, 1947); a hypnotist drives an innocent man to commit murder (Fear in the Night, 1947). In Otto Preminger’s Whirlpool (1950), a new synthesis emerges with José Ferrer as David Korvo, a hypnotist, astrologer, multilingual wit, urbane womanizer, and murderous blackmailer far more sophisticated than the psychoanalyst whose wife he hypnotizes into crime: a fashionable Caligari of the cocktail lounge.

Young Morey was perhaps too involved with the hardheaded practicalities of the family firm—a scrap metal business founded in 1890 by his immigrant grandfather that Morey’s business acumen helped to grow into a nationwide enterprise—to linger on such matters. The straightforward tone of his book suggests as much, as it skirts any hint of Svengali or Caligari. The Search for Bridey Murphy presents itself as the adventures of an all-American businessman from Pueblo, Colorado, with a no-nonsense approach to life. The opening finds him at work sometime in the early 1940s: “When the phone rang, it was night—a stormy night, at that—and I was at the office, in the middle of picking a winner in our slogan contest.” The call is from a traveler stranded by the storm, a client’s cousin. Morey takes him to a party, where it turns out that the traveler’s hobby is hypnosis, something Morey considers “beneath my intelligence.” A young woman consents to be hypnotized, and the ensuing demonstration demolishes his skepticism: “I was licked…. This girl was neither a fake nor a fool…. She filled all the specifications for the intelligent, normal, healthy, wholesome female.”

Here as elsewhere, normality, and whatever “specifications” might certify it, is the measuring stick for what can or cannot be believed. The normal world, as depicted, is a surface so thin as barely to be there. The client’s cousin is “pleasant, and personable…a real charmer”; Ginni Tighe is “a normal twentieth-century woman” with “normal duties as a housewife.” These silhouettes who work in offices, gather after hours in living rooms where they exchange “chatter…of the usual cocktail-party variety,” and are occasionally inconvenienced by thunderstorms resemble nothing so much as line drawings in an early 1950s advertisement in Life.

The incident at the party is a conversion experience, setting the materialistic Morey on a new path. He stops reading novels, even cuts back on trade journals: “I just couldn’t tear myself away from the hypnotism books; I was utterly enchanted.” His book is the relation of a progressive enchantment, marred only by one great disappointment: he finds he is incapable of being hypnotized. He is thus barred from experiencing a state in which a subject can “transcend his normal mental capacity, anesthetize any portion of his body, control pain.” (He makes no mention of one powerful reason for this: the lifelong aftereffects of a brutal high school prank in which he was tossed into shallow water, breaking his neck.) Despite extraordinary efforts—everything from narcosynthesis to shock therapy—he remains unable to “become master of his mind.”

Merely to be the hypnotist is to stay on the outside looking in. Morey seeks other paths, moving forward with boyish enthusiasm as one astonishing revelation follows another. He is steered on his way by unexpected guides: a Wall Street securities analyst, a government bureaucrat, an industrial engineer, all part of an underground of enlightened searchers. He learns of the legendary psychic healing powers of the “sleeping prophet” Edgar Cayce and finds wisdom in the pages of The Power Within and Phantasms of the Living. Dwelling on the notion of “imperishable conscious beings” migrating from one body to another, he is dazzled by the inescapably logical conclusion that “the mind must…be capable of reaching through time, because time, as we know it, is a function of space.”

Yet amid these speculative flights he never abandons his practical instincts. He wants tests, demonstrations, verified percentages: specifications, as for an electrified corral fence. He’s impatient to start tinkering, like Tom Swift building a spaceship in the backyard. Designing an experiment in telepathy, he selected five objects—“a drinking glass, a knife, a bar of soap, a coin, and a cigarette”—that are a condensed ode to modern American materiality, clues left over from a private eye novel. A veteran of sales pitches, he wants to sell the paranormal like a new model tractor, removing from hypnosis all trace of “the hocus-pocus variety: Svengali-Trilby; the ridiculous antics of stage performers; witchcraft and sorcery.”

The America of that moment wants to believe that the horrors of the war years have been left behind. Scientists are not mad; hypnotists are benevolent therapists. Morey wants to bring clairvoyance and trance into the hygienic light of day, Americanize and update them, strip away inherited European associations, the lore of necromancy and fortune-telling, the witch burnings, the heritage of antisemitism embodied in the figure of Svengali, the Russian pogroms from which his grandfather fled, all the warning shadows of the old continent. In that spirit he undertakes to lead Ginni Tighe into her prenatal life: even the journey backward along the pathways of reincarnation will be accomplished in a comfortable living room where death will be liberated from any hint of grief or fear. A thousand myths and folktales suggest that such a path cannot be traveled without cost, but not to a high-spirited experimenter equipped with a reel-to-reel tape recorder to anchor him in his own century.

We can read The Search for Bridey Murphy as a novel of the supernatural, written by a character in such a novel, a character under the illusion that he’s writing a how-to manual. For any outside observer the situation would be eerie—a direct communication from the dead could hardly be otherwise—but Morey insists that all this is not so uncanny, just an exciting opportunity. Yet he has tapped into something he can’t control, like an apprentice wizard inadvertently invoking a spirit. At midpoint, as the book becomes a dialogue in which a living interlocutor is privileged to ask questions of the dead, Bridey achieves an insidious dominance. Disembodied utterances become more real than the room where Morey listens to them, more real than the person uttering them. Bridey seems somehow still alive, “a saucy, rather flippant Irish girl…who manifested a distinct personality.”

He is delighted when Ginni, triggered by a posthypnotic suggestion, executes the “Morning Jig” that Bridey had talked about: “Her body became vibrantly alive; her feet were flying in a cute little dance.” Is this Ginni, or Bridey possessing Ginni? His reaction turns to panic when she resists emerging from the trance: “I was badly frightened…. It seemed as though she was going to insist upon retaining her identity as Bridey.” It is Morey who seems to have lost his way tiptoeing around in the astral plane. Bridey Murphy has become the true author of the book, with Morey her awed amanuensis: the hypnotist hypnotized.

Ginni registers only faintly in these pages. Introduced as “a vivacious brownette on the smallish side…trim, attractive, and one of the most sought-after partners at every dance,” she remains the perfect somnambule; after a session she “was not even aware of the words she had just spoken.” Meanwhile her husband accedes only reluctantly to the project and grows increasingly uneasy: “I just want to…be a regular guy; I don’t want to be dubbed a crackpot or a screwball.” He intervenes to keep the sessions short and is on hand to monitor what goes on. If this were a different kind of movie, one could envision Morey drawn into an erotic and controlling obsession with his subject, while her jealous husband edges toward violent confrontation.

But the implicit romance turns out to be of a more ghostly sort made for mist and theremin music, playing out—as in movies like The Ghost and Mrs. Muir (1947) or Portrait of Jennie (1948) or I’ll Never Forget You (1951)—across a hauntingly unbridgeable gulf of time. The persistence of memory beyond death cannot erase the underlying sadness, as Bridey is beaten down by life, comes at last to desire death, watches her own burial, and hovers among a shifting crowd of departed souls in “a place of waiting.” Morey does not acknowledge how dismal a vision is unfolding. The dead unknowingly persist along a hidden thread of continuity, but what does it connect to? As he questions Bridey about whether the living could possibly hear what the dead were saying, she interjects: “They won’t listen!” The emphatic punctuation marks this as the crucial moment: a voice is indeed breaking through a wall, whoever the voice might belong to and wherever it might be situated in time and space.

“I think it ruined both their lives,” a Pueblo resident speculated years later. No second book followed, nor any further publicly revealed explorations of reincarnation. Morey did not, as many another might have, found a cult or establish an institute of paranormal studies. Ginni, who had never sought publicity, was troubled by the hordes of intruders into her private life, the religiously motivated attacks, the accusations of fraud. Her marriage fell apart. She turned down countless commercial offers at the height of the Bridey mania—The Colgate Comedy Hour wanted her to reenact the trances on TV—although she can be seen as a guest on a 1965 episode of the game show To Tell the Truth. This long-running program featured three individuals each claiming to be the same person; a panel of celebrities quizzed them to weed out the two impostors. She maintains a dignified, confident air, but elsewhere admitted there had been difficult times: “Probably the main reason I’ve kept my cool is that I’m not convinced I was Bridey Murphy or anyone else.”

Morey was convinced. Heartened by floods of correspondence from readers eager to share their own experiences and theories, he threatened those who accused him of fraud with lawsuits. But the Bridey phenomenon triggered a personal disintegration, or perhaps more precisely laid bare what had always been there. His wife divorced him, alienated by abusive harangues and obsessive and sometimes outrageous behavior. (A visitor described him as “lying on the floor, ignoring his guests while restlessly clicking a TV remote, ‘just surfing the channels and cursing.’”) He sold the family business, devoted himself to investing, and became very rich. He also withdrew, moving into a small apartment he left rarely and finally not at all. Locals called him “the Howard Hughes of Pueblo.” The officially recorded cause of his death in 1999 was malnutrition. All he had ever needed from others, according to a memoir by his younger brother, “was respect, adoration, and a kind of Pavlovian submission to his control.” To shut the world out entirely may have been the final imposition of control.

Bridey never went away. Although in 1956 the debunkers seemed to have prevailed, a decade later she remained a beacon for a culture awash in the uncanny. The subterranean influence of The Search for Bridey Murphy, a book much investigated, much mocked, and rarely if ever out of print, outlasted Ginni and Morey. For a child in the Bible Belt it was “the first forbidden book I ever read.” For another early reader it led to a career of past life regression work. It opened many doors—to narratives of alien abduction, the recovered memories of innocents abused by Satanic cults, the sinister conspiracies of lizard-brained infiltrators. It had signaled a deep and pervasive yearning to leap, whether into the future or the past, beyond the intolerable constraints of cause and effect and materiality itself. And yet how many otherwise doubtful readers have not thought, if only for an instant, “What if, after all, it were really so?” The temptation is stubbornly persistent.
